title: Apply, map & String Accessor
blurb: apply, map and .str are the escape hatches from column thinking — reach for them when the logic is per value or per row.

cells.title: .str: vectorized string methods on a column
cells.body:
When a column holds strings, the .str accessor unlocks the whole string toolbox applied row by row — .str.lower(), .str.split(...), .str.contains(...) — without writing a loop. It is the middle ground between one big column expression and a Python for-loop: still row-wise logic, but expressed once, for the whole column.

Two habits pay off. First, chain small steps: .str.lower().str.split("@").str[-1] is three cheap, readable passes rather than one clever regex. Second, remember that every step maps missing values to missing values — the pipeline never crashes on a gap, it propagates it, which is exactly what you want when cleaning dirty exports.

demo.code:
import pandas as pd

emails = pd.Series(["Ana@Example.COM", "bo@corp.io"])
print(emails.str.lower().tolist())
print(emails.str.split("@").str[-1].tolist())

cells.title: apply with axis=1: when a row is the unit of logic
cells.body:
Some formulas need several columns of the same row at once — a shipping cost from weight and distance, a verdict from two test results. df.apply(fn, axis=1) hands your function each row (as a small Series you index by column name) and collects the returned values into a new Series aligned to the rows.

It is the most flexible tool in the box and the slowest way to do something a column expression could do — so treat it as a deliberate choice: row-level semantics that cannot be phrased column-wise. The result carries the frame's index, which is what makes it safe to assign back as a new column and keeps it aligned with the rows it was computed from.

cells.title: map: translate values through a dictionary
cells.body:
series.map(dictionary) replaces each value with its dictionary entry — codes to names, ids to categories. The decisive detail: keys missing from the dictionary become NaN, not an error. That silence is a feature when you follow it with .fillna("other"): "translate what you recognize, bucket the rest".

This is the vocabulary to reach for when the mapping is data — a lookup someone maintains — rather than logic you want to write. And after translating, the natural next question is "how many in each bucket?", which is .value_counts() territory — remembering that equal counts need a stated tie-break before the summary is a well-defined answer.

demo.code:
import pandas as pd

codes = pd.Series(["A", "B", "Z"])
mapping = {"A": "alpha", "B": "beta"}
cats = codes.map(mapping).fillna("other")
print(cats.tolist())
print(cats.value_counts().tolist())

exercise.title: Domains from a user list
exercise.statement:
A site stores its users in a table where each row is one user with columns user (str) and email (str). Every email contains exactly one @, like "Ana@Example.COM".

Implement email_domains(users) returning a Series named domain, aligned with the input rows (same order): for each user, the part of the email after the @, lowercased — so "Ana@Example.COM" yields "example.com".
constraints: Return a Series named 'domain' with one value per input row, in the input order
The domain is everything after the single '@', lowercased
Every email in the input contains exactly one '@' and is non-empty
Use the .str accessor — no Python-level loops over rows

examples.why: the part after the @ in the first email is 'Example.COM', which lowercases to 'example.com'
everything after the single @ counts as the domain, including dots inside it

exercise.starter:
import pandas as pd

def email_domains(users):
    """Return the lowercased email domain for each user.

    Series named 'domain', aligned with the input rows.
    """
    pass
hints: Which string operations do you need: something to normalize case, something to cut at a separator, and something to keep one piece of the cut?
Chain .str steps: .str.lower() normalizes the whole email; .str.split('@') cuts every row at the @; indexing the pieces with .str[-1] keeps the part after it.
return users['email'].str.lower().str.split('@').str[-1].rename('domain') — each step is one pass over the column and missing values (none here) would just stay missing.
exercise.reasoning: The .str accessor turns per-row string surgery into a column pipeline: lowercase normalizes case so that Example.COM and example.com stop being different domains, split cuts every value at the separator, and positional indexing (.str[-1]) picks the tail piece — robust even if the local part itself were empty. The order matters (lowercase then split, or split then lowercase the result — both work here because the @ itself has no case). What makes it idiomatic is that each step is stated once and applied to every row, keeping the logic data-parallel instead of loop-shaped.

exercise.title: Shipping cost, row by row
exercise.statement:
A courier prices each parcel with a per-row formula. Each row of parcels is one parcel with columns weight_kg (float), distance_km (float) and express (bool).

The cost of a parcel is:

  • base 2.0 plus 0.5 per kg, plus 0.1 per km;
  • the whole amount is doubled when express is True.

Implement shipping_costs(parcels) returning a Series named cost, aligned with the input rows (same order), every value rounded to 2 decimal places.
constraints: cost = (2.0 + 0.5 * weight_kg + 0.1 * distance_km), doubled when express is True
Return a Series named 'cost' with one value per input row, in the input order
Every value rounded to 2 decimal places
The formula reads several columns of the same row — this is a row-wise computation

examples.call: shipping_costs(parcels)  # 3 kg over 10 km, not express
examples.why: 2.0 + 0.5*3 + 0.1*10 = 4.5, and express does not double it
2.0 + 0.25 + 0.75 = 3.0 before doubling, and express doubles it to 6.0

exercise.starter:
import pandas as pd

def shipping_costs(parcels):
    """Return the per-parcel shipping cost.

    base 2.0 + 0.5/kg + 0.1/km, doubled for express;
    Series named 'cost', input row order, rounded to
    2 decimals.
    """
    pass
hints: The formula for one row needs weight, distance and the express flag TOGETHER. Can you write it as a function of a single row first, then get pandas to call it per row?
Define cost(row): c = 2.0 + 0.5*row['weight_kg'] + 0.1*row['distance_km']; double it when row['express']; then parcels.apply(cost, axis=1) runs it row by row.
def cost(row): c = 2.0 + 0.5 * row['weight_kg'] + 0.1 * row['distance_km']; return c * 2 if row['express'] else c — then return parcels.apply(cost, axis=1).round(2).rename('cost').
exercise.reasoning: This is the canonical case for axis=1: the unit of logic is a row, because no single column knows the answer — weight, distance and the express flag must meet in one place. apply(cost, axis=1) makes that meeting explicit: your function receives one row at a time (a Series indexed by column names) and returns one number, and pandas stitches the numbers back into a Series aligned with the rows. The final .round(2) is applied to the whole result at once — rounding is presentation, not part of the pricing formula, and doing it last keeps every intermediate exact.

exercise.title: Buckets and a ranked summary
exercise.statement:
Product codes come from many systems. Each row of products is one product with columns product (str) and code (str). A maintained dictionary code_to_category maps known codes to category names — but unmapped codes exist, and they all belong to a catch-all category called "other".

Implement category_summary(products, code_to_category):

  • translate each product's code to its category with map; codes missing from the dictionary become "other";
  • return a DataFrame with exactly the columns ["category", "count"]: one row per category with the number of products in it, sorted by count descending; categories with equal counts are ordered by category ascending.
constraints: Unmapped codes (not keys of code_to_category) all count as the category 'other'
Return a DataFrame with exactly the columns ['category', 'count'] in that order
count is the number of products per category
Rows sorted by count descending, ties by category ascending; the dictionary may be empty

examples.returns: DataFrame with columns ['category', 'count']: alpha 1, beta 1, other 1
examples.why: A and B translate through the dictionary, Z falls through to 'other', and the three-way tie at 1 sorts alphabetically

examples.returns: a single row: other N (N = number of products)
examples.why: an empty dictionary maps nothing, so every code lands in the catch-all bucket

exercise.starter:
import pandas as pd

def category_summary(products, code_to_category):
    """Return the ranked category counts.

    Codes are translated with map; unmapped codes read
    'other'. Columns ['category', 'count'], sorted by count
    descending, ties by category ascending.
    """
    pass
hints: What does series.map(dictionary) leave in the places where the code is not a key? What should those places become before you count?
cats = products['code'].map(code_to_category).fillna('other') translates and buckets in one line; then a value_counts-style count gives the per-category numbers.

counts = cats.value_counts().rename_axis('category').reset_index(name='count'); return counts.sort_values(['count', 'category'], ascending=[False, True]).reset_index(drop=True) — value_counts' own tie order is not a promise, the explicit sort is.
exercise.reasoning: Two ideas compose here. map treats a dictionary as data: translation is a lookup, not logic, and its silent NaN for unknown keys is exactly the hook for the "other" policy — fillna converts "unrecognized" into a first-class bucket instead of a crash. Then the summary: value_counts answers "how many per bucket", but its ordering of equal counts is an implementation detail, not a contract — so a deterministic answer re-sorts on ["count", "category"], the same tie-breaking discipline as any ranked report. Translate, bucket, count, then impose order: each step has one job.
